questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (8{t}^{3}+12)\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\cdot \frac{{t}^{4}}{4}+12t+C \\  & =2{t}^{4}+12t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $x(1)=10.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & =2(1)^{4}+12(1)+C \\ 10 & =2+12+C \\ C & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=2{t}^{4}+12t-4.
$$

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with velocity $v(t)=\frac{{t}^{2}-t}{4},$ where $t>0$ is the time. If the particle is at the position $x=-\frac{1}{6}$ when $t=2,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (\frac{{t}^{2}-t}{4})\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{12}{t}^{3}-\frac{1}{8}{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $x(2)=-\frac{1}{6}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{6} & =\frac{1}{12}(2)^{3}-\frac{1}{8}(2)^{2}+C \\ -\frac{1}{6} & =\frac{1}{6}+C \\ C & =-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{12}{t}^{3}-\frac{1}{8}{t}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3{t}^{2}-2)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{3}-2t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $x(0)=-1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & =(0)^{3}-2(0)+C \\ C & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is

$$
x(t)={t}^{3}-2t-1.
$$

questions.problem:
A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration 

$$
a(t)=\frac{8}{(t+2)^{3}},
$$

where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=0$ and velocity $v=1$ when $t=0,$ the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is

$x(t)=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \frac{8}{(t+2)^{3}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\int (t+2)^{-3}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\cdot \frac{(t+2)^{-2}}{-2}+C \\  & =-\frac{4}{(t+2)^{2}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =-\frac{4}{(0+2)^{2}}+C \\ 1 & =-\frac{4}{4}+C \\ 1 & =-1+C \\ C & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by 

$$
v(t)=-\frac{4}{(t+2)^{2}}+2.
$$

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (-\frac{4}{(t+2)^{2}}+2)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4\int (t+2)^{-2}\,\text{d}t+2\int \,\text{d}t \\  & =-4\cdot \frac{(t+2)^{-1}}{-1}+2t+K \\  & =\frac{4}{t+2}+2t+K.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =\frac{4}{0+2}+0+K \\ 0 & =2+K \\ K & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=\frac{4}{t+2}+2t-2.
$$

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=\frac{4}{(t+1)^{3}}$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=1$ and velocity $v=-\frac{1}{2}$ when $t=1$, calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \frac{4}{(t+1)^{3}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{2}{(t+1)^{2}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=-\frac{1}{2}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} & =-\frac{2}{(1+1)^{2}}+C \\ -\frac{1}{2} & =-\frac{1}{2}+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=-\frac{2}{(t+1)^{2}}.$ 

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (-\frac{2}{(t+1)^{2}})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{2}{t+1}+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K$, we use the fact that $x(1)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =\frac{2}{1+1}+K \\ 1 & =1+K \\ K & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=\frac{2}{t+1}.
$$

questions.problem:
A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)={e}^{3t},$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=0$ and velocity $v=1$ when $t=0,$ the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is

$x(t)=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int {e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{0}+C \\ 1 & =\frac{1}{3}+C \\ C & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}+\frac{2}{3}.$

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}+\frac{2}{3})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{2}{3}\int \,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{9}{e}^{3t}+\frac{2}{3}t+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K$, we use the fact that $x(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =\frac{1}{9}{e}^{0}+\frac{2}{3}(0)+K \\ 0 & =\frac{1}{9}+K \\ K & =-\frac{1}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{9}{e}^{3t}+\frac{2}{3}t-\frac{1}{9}.
$$

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=\frac{1}{16}$ and velocity $v=\frac{1}{4}$ when $t=\frac{\pi }{8}$, calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(\frac{\pi }{8})=\frac{1}{4}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{8})+C \\ \frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{4}+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).$ 

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(\frac{\pi }{8})=\frac{1}{16}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{16} & =-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{8})+C \\ \frac{1}{16} & =-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{16} & =0+C \\ K & =\frac{1}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{1}{16} \\  & =\frac{1}{16}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=t-2{t}^{4}$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=\frac{1}{10}$ and velocity $v=\frac{1}{10}$ when $t=1$, calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (t-2{t}^{4})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}-\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=\frac{1}{10}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{10} & =\frac{1}{2}(1)^{2}-\frac{2}{5}(1)^{5}+C \\ \frac{1}{10} & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{2}{5}+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}-\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5}.$ 

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}-\frac{2}{5}{t}^{5})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{t}^{3}-\frac{1}{15}{t}^{6}+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K$, we use the fact that $x(1)=\frac{1}{10}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{10} & =\frac{1}{6}(1)^{3}-\frac{1}{15}(1)^{6}+K \\ \frac{1}{10} & =\frac{1}{6}-\frac{1}{15}+K \\ \frac{1}{10} & =\frac{1}{10}+K \\ K & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{6}{t}^{3}-\frac{1}{15}{t}^{6}.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with velocity $v(t) = 2t+3t^2,$ where $t\geq 0$ is the time. If the particle is at the position $x=1$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the velocity to get $x(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2t+3{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{2}+{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $x(0) = 1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =(0)^{2}+(0)^{3}+C \\ C & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is

$$
x(t) = t^3+t^2+1.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t) = 1-2t,$ where $t\geq 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=1$ and velocity $v=2$ when $t=1,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t >0.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (1-2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =t-{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(1) = 2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =(1)-(1)^{2}+C \\ C & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t) = t-t^2 + 2.$

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (t-{t}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}+2t+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(1) = 1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =\frac{1}{2}(1)^{2}-\frac{1}{3}(1)^{3}+2(1)+K \\ K & =-\frac{7}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t) = \dfrac{1}{2}t^2-\dfrac{1}{3}t^3 +2t -\dfrac{7}{6}.
$$
